front: What is a trust?
back: A fiduciary relationship in which a trustee holds legal title to property under equitable duties to manage it for beneficiaries, created by a settlor who manifests intent (Prob. Code §§ 15200–15205).

front: Elements of a valid express trust.
back: Settlor with capacity; intent to create a trust; trust property; lawful purpose; ascertainable beneficiary (or charitable purpose). A trustee is not essential at creation.

front: Five ways to create a trust (§ 15200).
back: Declaration by the owner; inter vivos transfer to a trustee; transfer by will; exercise of a power of appointment; enforceable promise. No consideration required (§ 15208).

front: Which capacity test applies to a simple trust amendment in California?
back: The testamentary-capacity test of § 6100.5 where the amendment is no more complex than a will (Andersen v. Hunt); otherwise the decision-specific test of §§ 810–812.

front: Effect of precatory words ("I hope," "I wish") in a will.
back: Ordinarily no trust: the recipient takes an outright gift, unless the context shows the testator meant to impose an enforceable duty (§ 15201).

front: Can an expected inheritance be trust property?
back: No. A mere expectancy is not an existing property interest; it can become trust property only when it comes into existence and the settlor manifests intent again.

front: Heggstad rule.
back: A settlor-trustee's signed trust instrument listing an asset as trust property can make it trust property without a separate deed (Estate of Heggstad (1993)).

front: Which trust purposes are invalid?
back: Purposes that are illegal or against public policy (§ 15203), e.g., inducing crime, conditions intended to restrain marriage or encourage divorce.

front: Does a trust fail if the named trustee declines?
back: No. A trust never fails for want of a trustee; the court appoints a successor unless the settlor intended the trust only if that person served.

front: When does merger destroy a trust?
back: When the sole trustee is also the sole beneficiary of all interests. Remainder beneficiaries or a co-trustee prevent merger, so a typical living trust is valid.

front: Inter vivos vs. testamentary trust.
back: Inter vivos: created during life by declaration or transfer; funded assets avoid probate. Testamentary: created by will; effective at death; valid only if the will is valid; passes through probate.

front: Pour-over timing under § 6300.
back: Trust instrument may be executed before, concurrently with, or within 60 days after the will; trust may be unfunded; amendments before or after death apply; trust revoked before death → devise lapses.

front: Pour-over vs. incorporation by reference: key difference.
back: Pour-over (§ 6300) follows the trust as later amended; incorporation by reference captures only the document as it existed when the will was signed.

front: California default: is a trust revocable?
back: Yes. Unless the instrument expressly makes it irrevocable, the settlor may revoke (§ 15400). Traditional rule: irrevocable unless a power to revoke is reserved.

front: Two methods of revoking a revocable trust (§ 15401(a)).
back: (1) Any method stated in the instrument; (2) a signed writing, other than a will, delivered to the trustee during the settlor's lifetime.

front: When does the trust's own revocation method exclude the statutory method?
back: Only if the instrument explicitly makes its method the exclusive method (§ 15401(a)).

front: Can a later will revoke a California living trust?
back: Not by the statutory method: § 15401(a)(2) requires a writing other than a will. Only if the trust itself permits revocation by will. UTC § 602(c) contra (will referring to the trust).

front: Haggerty v. Thornton (2024) holding.
back: A revocable trust may be amended by the § 15401(a)(2) statutory revocation method (signed writing delivered to the trustee) unless the instrument provides a modification method and explicitly makes it exclusive.

front: What case did Haggerty disapprove?
back: King v. Lynch (2012), which required strict use of a trust's stated modification method.

front: Community property in a joint revocable trust: who may revoke, who must modify?
back: Either spouse alone may revoke as to CP; modification as to CP during marriage needs both spouses' joinder or consent (Fam. Code § 761).

front: May an agent under a general power of attorney amend the principal's trust?
back: Only if the power of attorney expressly authorizes it and the trust does not forbid it; a conservator needs court approval.

front: Totten trust.
back: Bank account "A in trust for B": revocable; A may withdraw during life; B takes the balance at A's death unless clear and convincing evidence of contrary intent; no will formalities.

front: Is a trust "for my grandchildren" valid if more may be born?
back: Yes. A class whose members can be determined is ascertainable.

front: Trust "for my friends": result?
back: Too indefinite for a private trust at common law; not charitable; fails → resulting trust to the settlor or estate (unless saved as a power of selection).

front: Charitable purposes.
back: Relief of poverty; advancement of education, religion, health; governmental or municipal purposes; other purposes beneficial to the community. Beneficiaries must be the public or an indefinite class.

front: Three special features of charitable trusts.
back: No ascertainable beneficiary needed; may last forever (no RAP limit on duration); enforced by the Attorney General.

front: Who may sue to enforce a charitable trust?
back: The Attorney General (Gov. Code § 12598), co-trustees and persons with a special interest; not members of the general public.

front: Elements of cy pres.
back: Valid charitable trust; specific purpose impossible, impracticable or illegal (Restatement (Third): or wasteful); general charitable intent; court directs funds to the purpose as near as possible.

front: What defeats cy pres?
back: A specific (not general) charitable intent, e.g., an express gift over on failure. Then the trust fails and a resulting trust returns the property to the settlor's estate.

front: Who chooses the new purpose under cy pres?
back: The court, choosing a purpose as near as possible to the original; it may reject the trustee's proposal if another purpose is closer.

front: Honorary (noncharitable purpose) trust in California.
back: Valid; the trustee may perform it for only 21 years (§ 15211).

front: Pet trust: duration and enforcement.
back: Valid (§ 15212); enforced by a person named in the instrument or appointed by the court; ends when no animal alive at the settlor's death remains alive, unless the instrument says otherwise.

front: Settlor and all beneficiaries agree to end an irrevocable trust. Result?
back: They may modify or terminate it without court approval, regardless of the trustee and of any material purpose (§ 15404).

front: Beneficiaries alone seek termination: California rule.
back: All must consent and petition; if a material purpose remains, the court may terminate only if the reason outweighs the interest in that purpose (§ 15403).

front: Claflin doctrine.
back: Beneficiaries cannot compel termination while a material purpose of the settlor remains unaccomplished (Claflin v. Claflin (Mass. 1889)).

front: Classic material purposes.
back: Spendthrift clause; discretionary or support provisions; postponed age of distribution; protective successive interests; keeping a family asset.

front: Changed-circumstances modification (§ 15409).
back: Court may modify administrative or dispositive terms or terminate if, owing to circumstances not known to or anticipated by the settlor, continuing would defeat or substantially impair the trust's purposes.

front: Uneconomic trust: when may the trustee terminate without a court?
back: If principal does not exceed $100,000 (SB 1127, 2024; was $40,000) and the instrument does not provide otherwise (§ 15408).

front: How does a trust end by its own terms?
back: Expiration of its term, accomplishment of its purpose, purpose becoming unlawful or impossible, or revocation; trustee winds up and distributes (§§ 15407, 15410).

front: Can a court combine two trusts?
back: Yes, if their terms are substantially similar and combining will not defeat or impair the purposes or beneficiaries' interests (§ 15411).

front: Statute of frauds for trusts of land (§ 15206).
back: Writing signed by the trustee (or authorized agent), or a conveyance signed by the settlor (or authorized agent), or operation of law.

front: Oral trust of personal property in California.
back: Valid, but existence and terms must be proved by clear and convincing evidence; the settlor's oral declaration alone is insufficient (§ 15207).

front: Secret trust: remedy.
back: Will makes an absolute gift; devisee promised to hold for another → extrinsic evidence admitted; constructive trust for the intended beneficiary.

front: Semi-secret trust: majority vs. modern result.
back: Will shows a trust but no terms. Majority: express trust fails → resulting trust for the estate. Modern (Restatement): constructive trust for the intended beneficiary.

front: USRAP test in California.
back: Valid if certain to vest or terminate within a life in being plus 21 years, or if it actually vests or terminates within 90 years; otherwise court reforms (§§ 21205, 21220).

front: Does the RAP limit charitable trusts?
back: Not their duration. A gift over from one charity to another is exempt; a gift over between private and charitable interests is subject to the rule.

front: When does a resulting trust arise on failure?
back: When an express trust fails in whole or part (no beneficiary, illegality, RAP, failed charity without cy pres) or has surplus after its purposes are met; property returns to settlor or estate.

front: Purchase-money resulting trust.
back: A pays, title to B → resulting trust for A presumed, unless gift or loan intended; gift presumed if B is A's spouse, child or natural object of bounty.

front: Constructive trust (Civ. Code § 2224).
back: One who gains a thing by fraud, accident, mistake, undue influence, violation of a trust or other wrongful act is an involuntary trustee for the person who would otherwise have had it.

front: Resulting vs. constructive trust.
back: Resulting: presumed intent (failed trust, purchase money); property back to settlor/payor. Constructive: remedy for wrongdoing; property to the person wronged.

front: Is a failed lifetime gift saved as a declaration of trust?
back: No, unless the donor intended to become a trustee; an imperfect gift is not recast as a trust.

front: Where does property of a failed testamentary trust go?
back: Into the residue; if the failed gift was residuary, to the other residuary takers; otherwise by intestacy (§ 21111).

front: Spendthrift clause: effect.
back: If the instrument restrains voluntary and involuntary transfer of income or principal, the beneficiary cannot assign and creditors cannot reach the interest before payment (§§ 15300–15301), subject to exceptions.

front: Can creditors reach trust money already paid to the beneficiary?
back: Yes. Once paid, it is the beneficiary's property. Principal that is due and payable may also be reached by court order (§ 15301(b)).

front: Support exception to spendthrift protection.
back: Child or spousal support judgments may be satisfied from payments due (or that the trustee decides to make) to the beneficiary (§ 15305).

front: Restitution exception (§ 15305.5).
back: A judgment for restitution or damages for a felony of which the beneficiary was convicted can reach the interest despite the spendthrift clause.

front: Public-support exception (§ 15306).
back: The State or a county may reach the interest to recover the cost of public support provided to the beneficiary, within statutory limits.

front: California's two routes for general creditors of a spendthrift beneficiary.
back: (1) Up to 25% of each payment, considering support needs (§ 15306.5); (2) amounts exceeding what the beneficiary needs for education and support (§ 15307). General law: general creditors barred.

front: Carmack v. Reynolds (2017).
back: The § 15306.5 25% figure is not an absolute limit on everything a creditor (there a bankruptcy trustee) may reach in a spendthrift trust.

front: Self-settled trust and the settlor's creditors.
back: Spendthrift restraint invalid as to the settlor; if discretionary, creditors reach the maximum the trustee could pay the settlor (§ 15304).

front: Discretionary trust and creditors.
back: Creditor cannot compel the trustee to exercise discretion (§ 15303); amounts the trustee decides to pay become subject to §§ 15305–15307; paying after notice of levy risks trustee liability.

front: Support trust protection.
back: Interest is protected to the extent necessary for the beneficiary's education or support, until paid (§ 15302); excess is reachable.

front: Discretionary vs. support trust.
back: Discretionary: no enforceable right to any amount, only to good-faith exercise of discretion. Support: enforceable right to what is needed for support.

front: Trustee's first duty on acceptance.
back: Administer according to the trust instrument and, except as validly varied, the statutory duties (§ 16000).

front: Trustee standard of care (§ 16040).
back: Reasonable care, skill and caution under the circumstances then prevailing that a prudent person acting in a like capacity would use; special skills must be used (§ 16014).

front: Duty of loyalty (§ 16002).
back: Administer the trust solely in the interest of the beneficiaries.

front: Is fair market value a defense to trustee self-dealing?
back: No. Under the no-further-inquiry rule, self-dealing is a breach regardless of fairness unless authorized by the instrument, consented to with full disclosure, or approved by the court (§ 16004(a)).

front: Presumption under § 16004(c).
back: A trustee–beneficiary transaction during the trust (or while influence remains) that gives the trustee an advantage is presumed a breach; burden of proof on the trustee; not for compensation agreements.

front: Trustee invests trust funds in his own start-up: which duties?
back: Loyalty (conflict of interest) and prudence (speculative, undiversified). Separate headings.

front: Duty of impartiality (§ 16003).
back: With two or more beneficiaries, deal impartially and invest and manage with regard to their differing interests (e.g., income vs. remainder).

front: Prudent investor rule (§ 16047).
back: Invest as a prudent investor would, considering purposes, terms, distribution needs; judge each decision in the context of the whole portfolio and an overall risk-return strategy.

front: Duty to diversify (§ 16048).
back: Diversify unless, under the circumstances, it is prudent not to (tax cost, special asset, valid retention clause).

front: Hindsight and the prudent investor rule.
back: Compliance is judged by the facts and circumstances at the time of the decision, not by the outcome (§ 16051).

front: Duties to preserve and make productive.
back: Take control of and preserve trust property, insure it, enforce claims, and make it productive consistent with the trust's purposes (§§ 16006–16011).

front: Is commingling a breach if no loss results?
back: Yes. The trustee must keep trust property separate and earmarked (§ 16009); losses that follow are charged to the trustee.

front: Co-trustees: default decision rule and duties.
back: Unanimity unless the instrument provides otherwise (§ 15620); each must participate and use reasonable care to prevent a co-trustee's breach and compel redress (§ 16013).

front: Delegation by a trustee.
back: May delegate investment and management functions a prudent trustee would, with care in selecting, setting terms and monitoring (§ 16052); may not abdicate the whole administration.

front: Duty to inform.
back: Keep beneficiaries reasonably informed; report on reasonable request; provide terms of an irrevocable trust on request (§§ 16060–16061.5).

front: When must a trustee account (§ 16062)?
back: At least annually, at termination, and on a change of trustee, to beneficiaries entitled to current distributions.

front: Is an account owed while the trust is revocable?
back: No (§ 16069); duties run to the settlor. (A later amendment to § 15800 requires annual accounts to remainder beneficiaries while the settlor is incompetent.)

front: Trust contest deadline after the settlor's death.
back: 120 days after service of the § 16061.7 notice, or 60 days after delivery of trust terms requested within the 120 days, whichever is later (§ 16061.8).

front: Trustee's notice deadline when a revocable trust becomes irrevocable on death.
back: Within 60 days, to each beneficiary and each heir (§ 16061.7).

front: Estate of Giraldin (2012).
back: After the settlor's death, beneficiaries have standing to sue the trustee for breaches committed while the trust was revocable; settlor's consent or direction is a defense.

front: Lawyer-trustee: may he take trustee fees and legal fees?
back: Not both, unless he waives trustee compensation or the court approves (§ 15687).

front: Sources of a trustee's powers.
back: The instrument, the statutes (§§ 16200 et seq.) unless limited, and implied powers needed to carry out the purposes; all exercised subject to fiduciary duties.

front: Standard for ordinary discretionary powers (§ 16080).
back: Not arbitrary; must be exercised reasonably, in good faith and consistent with the trust's terms and purposes.

front: "Sole and absolute discretion": what limits remain (§ 16081)?
back: Trustee must act in accordance with fiduciary principles, not in bad faith or in disregard of the trust's purposes; a trustee-beneficiary may pay himself only for health, education, support or maintenance.

front: What counts as abuse of discretion?
back: Bad faith, improper motive, failure to exercise judgment, or a decision outside the bounds of reasonable judgment.

front: Can a beneficiary sell her remainder interest?
back: Yes, unless a valid spendthrift clause restrains transfer.

front: Section 17200 petitions: examples.
back: Construe the instrument, determine validity, settle or compel accounts, instruct the trustee, modify or terminate, appoint or remove a trustee, compel redress, fix compensation.

front: Grounds to remove a trustee (§ 15642).
back: Breach of trust; insolvency or unfitness; co-trustee hostility impairing administration; failure to act; excessive compensation; disqualified sole trustee; other good cause.

front: Drafter or care custodian as sole trustee.
back: Removal ground under § 15642(b)(6) unless the court finds the settlor intended that person to serve and the intent was not the product of fraud or undue influence.

front: Is a petition to remove a trustee a "contest" under a no-contest clause?
back: No. No-contest clauses reach only direct contests without probable cause (and expressly covered ownership or creditor claims) (§ 21311).

front: Does § 21380 apply to trust amendments?
back: Yes. Gifts to the drafter, a fiduciary-transcriber, a care custodian of a dependent adult, and related persons are presumed the product of fraud or undue influence.

front: Can an omitted child take from a revocable trust?
back: Yes. Revocable trusts are testamentary instruments for the omitted spouse and omitted child statutes (§ 21601).

front: Remedies for breach of trust (§ 16420).
back: Compel performance; enjoin; surcharge (pay money or restore property); receiver or temporary trustee; remove; reduce or deny compensation; set aside acts; equitable lien or constructive trust; trace and recover (subject to § 18100).

front: Self-dealing remedies: beneficiaries' election.
back: Set aside the transaction and recover the property, or affirm and recover the trustee's profit and any loss, whichever is greater.

front: Constructive trust or equitable lien after tracing?
back: Constructive trust if the traced asset rose in value; equitable lien if it fell (plus deficiency).

front: Measure of trustee liability (§ 16440(a)).
back: Loss or depreciation caused, with interest; or profit the trustee made, with interest; or profit that would have accrued to the trust but for the breach.

front: When may the court excuse a trustee's liability?
back: If the trustee acted reasonably and in good faith under the circumstances known and excusing is equitable (§ 16440(b)).

front: When is a successor trustee liable for a predecessor's breach?
back: If the successor knew or should have known of it and improperly permitted it to continue or neglected to compel redress or delivery of trust property (§ 16403).

front: When is a co-trustee liable for the other's breach?
back: If she participated, improperly delegated, approved or concealed it, negligently enabled it, or failed to take reasonable steps to compel redress (§ 16402).

front: Limits on exculpatory clauses (§ 16461).
back: Cannot excuse breaches committed intentionally, with gross negligence, in bad faith or with reckless indifference, or profit the trustee derived from a breach.

front: When is a beneficiary's consent or release ineffective?
back: If induced by improper conduct, the beneficiary lacked capacity, or the beneficiary did not know the material facts or her rights (§§ 16463–16465).

front: Limitations period for breach of trust (§ 16460).
back: Three years after receiving an account or report that adequately discloses the claim; otherwise three years after the beneficiary discovered or reasonably should have discovered it.

front: Trustee dies after misusing trust funds. Remedy?
back: The claim survives; the successor trustee should pursue the deceased trustee's estate for repayment with interest (CCP § 377.20; § 16403).

front: Beneficiary urged the breach: consequences.
back: She cannot sue for it; her interest may be impounded to indemnify the trust or other beneficiaries; overpayments must be restored.

front: Is a beneficiary personally liable to a person injured on trust property?
back: No, not merely as beneficiary; the claim runs against the trust through the trustee, and the trustee personally if at fault.

front: Trustee's personal liability on trust contracts (§ 18000).
back: None on a contract properly made in the fiduciary capacity, unless the trustee failed to reveal the capacity and identify the trust. Common law: personally liable unless the contract excluded it.

front: Trustee's personal liability for torts in administration.
back: Only if personally at fault (§§ 18001–18002); claims may be asserted against the trust by suing the trustee in a representative capacity (§ 18004).

front: Settlor's creditors and a revocable trust during the settlor's life.
back: Trust property is subject to the settlor's creditors to the extent of the power of revocation (§ 18200); a spendthrift clause does not help.

front: Settlor's creditors after death: revocable trust.
back: Property that was revocable at death is subject to creditors and administration expenses to the extent the probate estate is inadequate (§ 19001).

front: Liability of a third party who knowingly helps a trustee breach.
back: Liable for the resulting loss; holds any trust property received on constructive trust.

front: Protection of a third party who buys from a trustee (§ 18100).
back: Protected if in good faith, for value and without actual knowledge that the trustee is exceeding or improperly exercising powers; no duty to inquire; constructive notice does not defeat protection.

front: Donee of wrongfully transferred trust property.
back: Takes subject to the beneficiaries' claim (no value given) and must restore the property or its value.

front: Probate Code § 859.
back: A person who in bad faith wrongfully took, concealed or disposed of trust property (or took it by undue influence or elder financial abuse) is liable for twice the value of the property recovered, and possibly attorney's fees.

front: Which law to write on a Trusts essay?
back: Read the call. If it says California law, lead with the Probate Code. If silent, lead with general principles and add the California section, giving both where they differ.

front: Most common Trusts crossover partner on the California bar.
back: Wills and Succession (6 times, 2012–2026); once also with Community Property.
